title: Heart Racing After Drinking: Why It Happens and When to Worry
excerpt: Why your heart races after drinking or the morning after, how to tell a fast beat from an irregular one, holiday heart and AFib, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why your heart races after drinking, how to calm it, holiday heart and AFib explained, and the warning signs that mean you should see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a faster heartbeat after drinking is common and, in most healthy people, harmless and temporary. Alcohol widens your blood vessels, dehydrates you, and stirs up your stress hormones, and your heart speeds up to compensate. The next morning, a hangover adds poor sleep, low fluids, and sometimes too much coffee on top. That usually settles within hours as you rehydrate and rest. But alcohol can also trigger a real heart rhythm problem called atrial fibrillation (AFib), sometimes nicknamed "holiday heart," and a racing heart can also be a sign of alcohol withdrawal in people who drink heavily. This guide explains what's going on, what you can do about it, and the specific signs that mean you should get medical help rather than wait it out.

> **When to see a doctor or call 911:** Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if your racing heart comes with **chest pain or pressure, fainting or nearly fainting, severe shortness of breath, confusion, or a heart rate that stays very fast (for example, over about 120 to 130 beats per minute) while you're resting**. Get medical care the same day if the pounding or fluttering **lasts more than a few hours**, your pulse feels **irregular** (skipping, chaotic, or uneven rather than just fast), it happens **every time you drink**, or you have a known heart condition, high blood pressure, or thyroid disease. If you drink heavily most days and your heart races along with **shaking, sweating, anxiety, or seeing or hearing things** as the alcohol wears off, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Don't try to ride it out alone, and don't drink more to make it stop. Get medical help. **This article is general information, not medical advice.**

## Why Your Heart Races After Drinking

Your heart rate is controlled by a balance between two systems. One is the "rest and digest" side of your nervous system, which slows things down. The other is the "fight or flight" side, which speeds things up using adrenaline and related hormones. Alcohol pushes on that balance in several ways at once, so a racing heart usually has more than one cause.

### 1. Alcohol widens your blood vessels

Alcohol relaxes the walls of your blood vessels. That's why your face can flush and you feel warm. When your vessels widen, your blood pressure tends to dip. Your body responds by speeding up your heart to keep enough blood flowing to your brain and organs. This is a normal reflex, and it's one reason your pulse can climb within an hour or so of a couple of drinks.

### 2. It switches on your stress response

Even though alcohol feels relaxing, studies of heart rate variability (a measure of how flexibly your heart responds to your nervous system) show that drinking tilts the balance toward the "fight or flight" side. A well-known German study of people at Munich's Oktoberfest, called MunichBREW and published in the *European Heart Journal* in 2017, measured breath alcohol and heart rhythms in thousands of festival-goers. Higher breath alcohol was linked with a faster heart rate, a shift toward the stress side of the nervous system, and more episodes of abnormal rhythm. In plain terms: the more you'd had to drink, the more wound-up your heart looked.

### 3. Dehydration

Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin) that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. So you pee more than you drink, and you can wake up with less fluid in your bloodstream. Less fluid means less blood volume, and your heart beats faster to move what's left. This is the same reason your pulse rises when you're sick with a stomach bug or out in the heat. If you also vomited or had diarrhea, the effect is bigger.

### 4. Electrolyte shifts

The extra urination also costs you minerals like potassium and magnesium. These minerals help control the electrical signals that keep your heart beating in a steady rhythm. Big drops are uncommon after a normal night out, but low levels are more likely after heavy or repeated drinking, after vomiting, or in people who don't eat much while they drink. Low potassium or magnesium can make skipped beats and palpitations more likely. For a closer look, see our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).

### 5. Low blood sugar

Your liver normally releases sugar into your blood between meals. While it's busy breaking down alcohol, it's less able to do that. If you drank without eating, your blood sugar can dip overnight or the next morning. Your body responds to low blood sugar by releasing adrenaline, which can make you shaky, sweaty, and give you a pounding heart.

### 6. Acetaldehyde and the "flush"

When your liver breaks down alcohol, the first by-product is acetaldehyde, a toxic chemical that's later converted into harmless acetate. Acetaldehyde dilates blood vessels and raises heart rate. Some people, especially many people of East Asian descent, carry a gene variant (in an enzyme called ALDH2) that clears acetaldehyde slowly. For them, even one drink can cause a red face, a fast heartbeat, and a pounding headache. If that sounds like you, the racing heart is your body telling you acetaldehyde is building up, and it's a sign to drink less, not to push through.

### 7. Poor sleep

Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night. As alcohol levels fall, your body goes through a small rebound of alertness, and many people wake around 3 or 4 a.m. with a fast heartbeat, sweating, and racing thoughts. Short, broken sleep also leaves your stress hormones higher the next day. Our article on [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) explains this rebound in more detail.

### 8. Hangover anxiety ("hangxiety")

The morning after drinking, many people feel anxious, jittery, or full of dread. Part of that is the brain readjusting after alcohol has boosted its calming chemical (GABA) and dampened its excitatory one (glutamate). When the alcohol is gone, the balance swings the other way for a while. Anxiety and a racing heart feed each other: you notice your heartbeat, you worry about it, and the worry speeds it up further. Our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) covers this cycle and how to break it.

### 9. What you drank it with

A lot of next-day palpitations come from things other than the alcohol itself:

- **Energy drinks and caffeine mixers** (vodka Red Bull, espresso martinis, rum and cola) add a stimulant on top of the alcohol. Caffeine can mask how drunk you feel, so people often drink more.
- **Morning-after coffee** on an empty stomach and a dehydrated body can push an already-fast heart higher.
- **Nicotine** from cigarettes or vapes, which many people use more when they drink, raises heart rate.
- **Recreational drugs**, especially stimulants like cocaine, are a dangerous combination with alcohol and a real cause of serious heart rhythm problems and heart attacks. If you've used them and your heart is racing, especially with chest pain, get emergency care.
- **Decongestants** such as pseudoephedrine, found in some cold medicines, can also raise heart rate.

## Holiday Heart Syndrome: When Drinking Triggers AFib

Most fast heartbeats after drinking are "sinus tachycardia," which just means your normal heart rhythm running fast. It's regular, like a drum played quickly. But sometimes alcohol triggers an actual rhythm problem, most often atrial fibrillation.

In AFib, the upper chambers of the heart stop beating in a coordinated way and instead quiver chaotically. The pulse becomes irregular as well as fast. People describe it as fluttering, flopping, a fish flapping in the chest, or a heartbeat that feels "all over the place." Some people feel breathless, tired, dizzy, or have chest discomfort. Some feel very little.

The term "holiday heart syndrome" was coined by cardiologist Philip Ettinger and colleagues in a 1978 paper in the *American Heart Journal*. They described otherwise healthy people who turned up with rhythm problems after weekend or holiday binge drinking, with the episodes often clustering around holidays such as Christmas and New Year.

Later research has backed up the link:

- **The Oktoberfest study** mentioned above found that acute alcohol intake was associated with more abnormal heart rhythms, mostly a fast but otherwise normal rhythm, in a dose-related way.
- **A 2021 study in the *Annals of Internal Medicine*** by researchers at the University of California, San Francisco, had people with a history of AFib wear heart monitors and alcohol sensors. Drinking was followed by a higher chance of an AFib episode within the next few hours, and the risk rose with more drinks. This was some of the clearest evidence that alcohol can act as a short-term trigger, not just a long-term risk factor.
- **A 2020 randomized trial in the *New England Journal of Medicine*** from Australia found that regular drinkers with AFib who cut out alcohol had fewer AFib recurrences than those who kept drinking.

For many people, an alcohol-triggered episode of AFib stops on its own within a day or so. But AFib is not something to self-diagnose or dismiss. While the heart is out of rhythm, blood can pool in the upper chambers, which raises the risk of clots and stroke. A very fast irregular rhythm can also strain the heart. **If your pulse is irregular rather than just fast, get checked, ideally while it's happening so a doctor can record it.**

### How to tell a fast rhythm from an irregular one

You can check your pulse at your wrist (thumb side) or on the side of your neck. Count the beats for 30 seconds and double it.

| What you notice | What it might be | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Fast but steady, like a quick drumbeat, under about 100 to 110 at rest, easing as you hydrate | Normal rhythm running fast from dehydration, alcohol, caffeine, or anxiety | Rest, fluids, food, skip the caffeine, recheck in an hour or two |
| Occasional skipped or "thumping" beats with a normal rhythm in between | Extra beats (ectopic beats), common after drinking and usually harmless | Same as above; mention it to a doctor if it's frequent or new |
| Irregular, chaotic, no steady pattern | Possible atrial fibrillation or another rhythm problem | Get medical care the same day; call 911 if you have chest pain, fainting, or severe breathlessness |
| Very fast (over about 120 to 130) at rest and not settling, or with chest pain, fainting, or confusion | Possible serious rhythm problem or other emergency | Call 911 |

Many smartwatches can take a single-lead ECG and flag a possible irregular rhythm. A reading is not a diagnosis, but recording it and showing it to a doctor can be genuinely useful, because by the time you get to a clinic the episode may be over.

## A Racing Heart and Alcohol Withdrawal

This section matters if you drink heavily on most days. If that's not you, a racing heart the morning after a single night out is far more likely to be dehydration, poor sleep, and hangover anxiety.

When someone has been drinking heavily for a long stretch, their brain adapts to having alcohol around. If they suddenly stop or cut back sharply, the nervous system can become overactive. Early withdrawal signs often begin within roughly 6 to 24 hours of the last drink and can include a fast heartbeat, shaking hands, sweating, anxiety, nausea, and trouble sleeping. In some people, withdrawal progresses to seizures or a dangerous state called delirium tremens, with confusion, fever, and hallucinations.

Withdrawal can be risky enough that medical guidance is clear: people who are physically dependent on alcohol should not stop suddenly without medical support. If your racing heart comes with shakes and sweats as the alcohol wears off, and you've been drinking heavily for days or weeks, talk to a doctor or go to urgent care. Drinking more to make the symptoms go away is not a fix; it keeps the cycle running.

## What to Do Right Now If Your Heart Is Racing

If you've checked the warning signs above and none apply, these steps usually help a normal fast heartbeat settle:

1. **Sit or lie down and slow your breathing.** Breathe in through your nose for about four seconds and out through your mouth for about six. Longer out-breaths nudge your nervous system toward the calming side. Anxiety makes a racing heart worse, and this is the quickest way to break the loop.
2. **Drink water.** Sip steadily rather than chugging. If you vomited or had diarrhea, an oral rehydration drink with sodium and potassium helps you hold on to fluid better than plain water.
3. **Eat something.** A simple meal with some carbohydrates and salt, like toast, crackers, eggs, soup, or a banana, can lift low blood sugar and replace electrolytes.
4. **Skip caffeine, nicotine, and energy drinks** for the morning. If you rely on coffee, have a small cup after food rather than a large one on an empty stomach.
5. **Don't take decongestants or stimulants**, and don't use another drink to "take the edge off."
6. **Recheck your pulse in an hour or two.** A normal fast heartbeat from a hangover usually drifts down as you rehydrate and rest. If it isn't easing, is irregular, or you feel worse, get checked.
7. **Rest, but don't panic.** Most people feel noticeably better by the afternoon. A short walk is fine once you feel steadier; save hard exercise for another day, because pushing your heart rate up while dehydrated is not helpful.

Some people are told about "vagal maneuvers," such as bearing down as if straining, to slow certain fast rhythms. These are best learned from a doctor for a diagnosed condition. Don't rely on them as a substitute for getting checked.

## How Long Does a Racing Heart After Drinking Last?

For most people, a fast heartbeat linked to drinking peaks during the evening or the early hours, when alcohol levels are falling and sleep is disrupted. The next-day version usually eases over a few hours as you rehydrate, eat, and calm down, and is often gone by the afternoon or evening.

It's worth getting checked if:

- It lasts more than a few hours despite rest and fluids.
- It keeps coming back the next day or two.
- It happens after small amounts of alcohol, or every time you drink.
- Your rhythm feels irregular.

An episode of alcohol-triggered AFib can last longer than a simple fast heartbeat, from minutes to a day or more. Withdrawal-related symptoms in heavy drinkers often peak between one and three days after the last drink. Neither of these is a "wait and see" situation.

## Who Is More Likely to Get Palpitations From Alcohol?

You may be more prone to a racing heart after drinking if you:

- **Binge drink**, meaning several drinks in a short space of time. The amount matters, and so does the speed.
- **Mix alcohol with caffeine or energy drinks.**
- **Drink on an empty stomach** or skip meals the next day.
- **Have the alcohol flush reaction** (red face, fast heartbeat after one drink).
- **Have an existing heart condition**, high blood pressure, an overactive thyroid, or a history of AFib.
- **Have anxiety or panic attacks**, since alcohol's rebound effect can set them off.
- **Take certain medicines**, including some ADHD stimulants, decongestants, asthma inhalers, or thyroid medication. Check with a pharmacist about alcohol if you take any regular medicine.
- **Sleep poorly or drink late into the night.**

If you have high blood pressure, our guide on [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) covers how drinking affects it over time.

## Is a Racing Heart After Drinking Dangerous Long-Term?

An occasional fast heartbeat after a big night, in someone with a healthy heart, is generally not a sign of lasting damage. The bigger picture is what your drinking pattern looks like over months and years.

Research on long-term drinking consistently links heavy and regular drinking with a higher risk of AFib, high blood pressure, and, at very heavy levels, a weakening of the heart muscle called alcoholic cardiomyopathy. Studies over the past decade have also found that the risk of AFib rises even with moderate regular drinking, not just heavy drinking. The older idea that a drink a day is good for your heart has been questioned as newer research has accounted for problems in the earlier studies. For a fuller picture, see our [alcohol and heart health guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-heart-health-complete-cardiovascular-guide-2025).

So a racing heart is useful information. If it happens now and then after you've overdone it, it's a reminder to pace yourself. If it happens often, or after only a drink or two, it's worth a conversation with a doctor, who may suggest a heart monitor, blood tests for thyroid and electrolytes, or a blood pressure check.

## How to Prevent It Next Time

The steps with the best support are the simple ones:

- **Drink less, and drink slower.** Since the effects on heart rhythm rise with the amount you drink, fewer drinks spread over more time is the single most effective change. Aim for no more than about one standard drink an hour.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows your pace and limits dehydration.
- **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption and helps keep blood sugar steadier.
- **Avoid caffeine-alcohol mixes**, especially energy drinks.
- **Stop drinking a few hours before bed** so more of the alcohol has cleared before you sleep.
- **Have a plan for the next morning:** water by the bed, an easy breakfast, and a small coffee only after food.
- **Know your triggers.** If you notice palpitations every time you drink a certain amount, or a certain kind of drink, take that seriously.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through these habits in more depth.

### Where supplements fit (and where they don't)

No supplement treats or prevents heart rhythm problems, and none makes it safe to drink more. If you have palpitations, AFib, or a heart condition, see a doctor rather than reaching for a pill, and check with them before taking anything new.

That said, some people use supplements as part of their wider hangover routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts in the brain. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, and there is no good evidence that it prevents a racing heart or protects against alcohol's effects on heart rhythm. If you want to try DHM for general hangover support, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare brands. Treat it as an add-on to drinking less and staying hydrated, not a replacement.

## The Bottom Line

- A fast heartbeat after drinking is common. Widened blood vessels, dehydration, stress hormones, low blood sugar, poor sleep, caffeine, and hangover anxiety all play a part.
- It usually settles within a few hours with rest, fluids, food, and slow breathing.
- Alcohol can trigger atrial fibrillation ("holiday heart"), which makes the pulse irregular as well as fast. An irregular pulse needs a medical check.
- Call 911 for chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness, confusion, or a very fast resting heart rate that won't settle.
- If you drink heavily most days and your heart races with shaking and sweating as alcohol wears off, that may be withdrawal. Get medical help rather than drinking more.
- The best prevention is drinking less, drinking slower, eating, hydrating, and skipping caffeine-alcohol mixes.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why is my heart racing after drinking alcohol?**

Alcohol widens your blood vessels, which can lower blood pressure and make your heart speed up to compensate. It also dehydrates you, shifts your nervous system toward the stress response, can lower blood sugar, and disrupts sleep. The next day, hangover anxiety and caffeine can add to it. In most healthy people it's temporary, but an irregular pulse, chest pain, or fainting needs medical attention.

**Is it normal for your heart to race the day after drinking?**

A somewhat faster heartbeat the morning after a night of drinking is common, mostly from dehydration, broken sleep, and the rebound anxiety some people feel as alcohol leaves the body. It usually eases within a few hours with water, food, and rest. If it lasts more than a few hours, feels irregular, or comes with chest pain, dizziness, or breathlessness, get checked.

**What is holiday heart syndrome?**

Holiday heart syndrome is a term from a 1978 medical paper describing heart rhythm problems, most often atrial fibrillation, triggered by binge drinking in people who otherwise seemed healthy. The name comes from the way cases clustered around holidays and weekends. Episodes often stop on their own, but atrial fibrillation raises stroke risk while it lasts, so anyone with an irregular heartbeat after drinking should see a doctor.

**When should I worry about heart palpitations after drinking?**

Call 911 if you have chest pain or pressure, fainting, severe shortness of breath, confusion, or a very fast resting heart rate that isn't settling. Get seen the same day if your pulse is irregular, the racing lasts more than a few hours, it happens every time you drink, or you have a heart condition. If you drink heavily most days and also have shaking and sweating, it may be withdrawal and needs medical care.

**How long does a racing heart last after drinking?**

A simple fast heartbeat from drinking usually peaks overnight or early the next morning and eases over a few hours as you rehydrate, eat, and rest. It's often gone by the afternoon. If it lasts longer than a few hours, keeps coming back, or feels irregular, see a doctor, since an alcohol-triggered rhythm problem can last longer and is worth recording while it's happening.

**How do I calm my racing heart after drinking?**

Sit or lie down and breathe slowly, making each breath out longer than the breath in. Sip water or an oral rehydration drink, eat a simple meal with some salt and carbohydrates, and skip coffee, energy drinks, and nicotine for the morning. Recheck your pulse after an hour or two. If it's irregular, not easing, or you have warning symptoms like chest pain, get medical help.

**Can one drink make your heart race?**

Yes, for some people. Those with the alcohol flush reaction, which is common in people of East Asian descent, clear acetaldehyde slowly and can get a red face and fast heartbeat after a single drink. People with anxiety, heart rhythm conditions, or who mix alcohol with caffeine may also notice it after small amounts. If it happens to you regularly with just one drink, mention it to your doctor.

**Can a racing heart after drinking be alcohol withdrawal?**

It can be in people who have been drinking heavily for days or weeks. Withdrawal often starts within about 6 to 24 hours of the last drink and can bring a fast heartbeat, shaking, sweating, anxiety, and nausea, and it can become dangerous. For someone who drinks socially and had one big night, a racing heart is far more likely to be dehydration and poor sleep. If you think it might be withdrawal, get medical help and don't stop heavy drinking suddenly without support.
